items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we wish to find the number of distinct permutations of the following letters:
[MATH: a, \qquad a, \qquad b, \qquad b, \qquad c]
There are two [MATH: a]'s, two [MATH: b]'s, and one [MATH: c,] and a total of [MATH: 5] letters.

Content:
First, recall that there are [MATH: 5!] ways of arranging a sequence of [MATH: 5] objects. However, some arrangements will be the same since we have repeated letters. For example, we get the same final arrangement by swapping the first and the second positions in the sequence above.

Content:
If we were to list all arrangements of the above sequence by shuffling only the repeated letters among themselves (using suffixes to track the repeated letters), we get the following:

Content:
[MATH: a_{1}, a_{2}, b_{1}, b_{2}, c; a_{2}, a_{1}, b_{1}, b_{2}, c; a_{1}, a_{2}, b_{2}, b_{1}, c; a_{2}, a_{1}, b_{2}, b_{1}, c]

Content:
Rearranging the [MATH: a]'s among themselves in any way will not change the final result, nor will rearranging the [MATH: b]'s and [MATH: c]'s.

Content:
Notice that we have [MATH: 4] ways of rearranging the letters among themselves:

Content:
- Since we have two [MATH: a]'s, there are [MATH: 2!] ways of arranging them.
- Since we have two [MATH: b]'s, there are [MATH: 2!] ways of arranging them.
- Since we have one [MATH: c], there is only [MATH: 1!=1] way of arranging it.

Content:
In total, there are [MATH: 2! \cdot 2! \cdot 1! = 4] ways of arranging letters of our sequence if we can shuffle only the same letters among themselves.

Content:
So, to find the number of distinct permutations of our sequence, we need to divide the total number of arrangements [MATH: (5!)] by the number of arrangements that do not change anything ([MATH: 2! \cdot 2! \cdot 1!]):

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{5!}{2! \cdot 2! \cdot 1!} = 30]

Content:
Therefore, there are [MATH: 30] distinct ways of arranging this sequence of letters.

items.title: Computing the Number of Permutations With One Repeated Item

sections.normalized_html: How many distinct permutations can be formed using all letters of the word "FREE"?
sections.readable_text: How many distinct permutations can be formed using all letters of the word "FREE"?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The number of permutations of [MATH: N] symbols with [MATH: m_1, m_2,...,m_k] repeated symbols is given by the multinomial formula:

[MATH: (N; m_{1}, m_{2}, …, m_{k}) = (N!)/(m_{1}!m_{2}!…m_{k}!),]

where [MATH: m_1 + m_2 + \ldots + m_k = N.]

Here, the word "FREE" has [MATH: 4] letters in total, so [MATH: N=4.]

  • The letter "F" appears once, so [MATH: m_1=1.]

  • The letter "R" appears once, so [MATH: m_2=1.]

  • The letter "E" appears twice, so [MATH: m_3=2.]

Therefore, the number of permutations is given by

[MATH: (4; 1, 1, 2)|= (4!)/(1!1!2!); = (4 × 3 × 2 × 1)/(2); = 12.]

Item 12 — Tutorial: The Relationship Between the Multinomial and Binomial Formulas

Content:
The binomial formula is a special case of the multinomial formula. According to the binomial formula, the number of ways that we can choose [MATH: r] objects from a set of [MATH: N] objects is
[MATH: \binom{N}{r} = \dfrac{N!}{r! (N-r)!}.]
If we let [MATH: m_1 = r] and [MATH: m_2 = N-r,] then we have
[MATH: \binom{N}{r} = \dfrac{N!}{r! (N-r)!} = \dfrac{N!}{m_1! \, m_2!} = \binom{N}{m_1, m_2}.]
